claims.text: A 50–100 nm Ni interlayer can be conformally deposited at W/Cu interfaces by electrodeposition or sputter deposition.
Vacuum annealing at approximately 800 K for about 1 hour will produce controlled interdiffusion at the Ni-modified W/Cu interface.
The Ni interlayer and annealing treatment will form a graded W–Ni–Cu interfacial region.
The graded W–Ni–Cu region will reduce lattice mismatch at the interface.
The graded interfacial region will reduce interfacial stress concentrations.
The graded interfacial region will ensure coherent bonding and improve interfacial stability.
A Ni interlayer enhances wetting between W and Cu.
A Ni interlayer promotes controlled interdiffusion between the interfacial constituents.
The Ni-derived graded interface reduces the driving force for phase separation.
Alleviating local stress peaks reduces interfacial void nucleation during thermal cycling and irradiation.
The treatment mitigates rapid diffusion during thermal cycling and irradiation.
The Ni-interlayer-treated composite will have fewer interfacial voids and less phase segregation than an untreated W–Cu composite.
The Ni-interlayer-treated composite will have higher thermal conductivity than the untreated composite.
The Ni-interlayer-treated composite will have improved mechanical integrity relative to the untreated composite.
Untreated W–Cu composites undergo phase separation and interfacial void formation during thermal cycling and irradiation.
Phase separation and interfacial void formation degrade the thermal conductivity of untreated W–Cu composites.
The proposed treatment remains effective at service temperatures up to approximately 1000 K.
The proposed treatment remains effective at irradiation doses of approximately 1–2 dpa.
Maintaining a 50–100 nm Ni thickness and annealing near 800 K in vacuum avoids uncontrolled intermetallic formation.
Small deviations from the proposed annealing conditions may produce undesirable brittle intermetallic phases.
